ref: 1.10.1 (ANF/Massuet numbering; Harvey p. 90 heading "Expositio praedicationis veritatis" / "CAP. II")
greek: ECCLESIA enim [et quidem] per universum orbem usque ad fines terrae [dis]seminata, et ab Apostolis, et discipulis eorum accepit eam fidem, quae est in unum Deum, Patrem omnipotentem, qui fecit caelum et terram, et mare, et omnia quae in eis sunt: et in unum Christum Jesum filium Dei, incarnatum pro nostra salute: et in Spiritum Sanctum, qui per Prophetas praedicavit [Latin continues on p. 91; not transcribed].
greek_edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857, vol. 1 (Latin; archive.org item sanctiirenilibr01irengoog). Latin read from the Google djvu OCR and checked against the page image (PDF page) by eye; OCR may still err in individual letters. Harvey also prints the Greek of Epiphanius for this clause above it on p. 90 (OCR: "εἰς ἕνα Θεὸν Πατέρα παντοκράτορα", "εἰς ἕνα Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν, τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ", "εἰς Πνεῦμα ἅγιον"); not verified letter by letter.
english: "The Church, though dispersed throughout the whole world, even to the ends of the earth, has received from the apostles and their disciples this faith: [She believes] in one God, the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are in them; and in one Christ Jesus, the Son of God, who became incarnate for our salvation; and in the Holy Spirit, who proclaimed through the prophets the dispensations of God, ..."
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, Buffalo 1885; New Advent text revised by Kevin Knight)
what_it_says: The Church holds one God the Father Almighty, one Christ Jesus the Son of God, and the Holy Spirit, a three-part confession that Irenaeus calls the Church's faith.
limits: A baptismal-type summary: it names Father, Son and Spirit together but does not use homoousios or define their mutual relation; the Son is "incarnate", the Spirit is the prophetic speaker. Latin continues onto p. 91, not read in full here.

ref: 1.22.1 (ANF/Massuet); Harvey pp. 188-189, Massuet margin "MASS. I. xxii. 1"
greek: [p. 188] Cum teneamus autem nos regulam veritatis, id est, quia sit unus Deus omnipotens, qui omnia condidit per Verbum suum, et aptavit, et fecit ex eo, quod non erat, ad hoc ut sint omnia [p. 189] ... non per angelos, neque per virtutes aliquas abscissas ab ejus sententia: nihil enim indiget omnium Deus; sed per Verbum et Spiritum suum omnia faciens, et disponens, et gubernans, et omnibus esse praestans: hic qui mundum fecit ... hic Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi, quemadmodum ostendemus:
greek_edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857, vol. 1 (Latin; archive.org item sanctiirenilibr01irengoog). Latin only (no Greek printed for this paragraph on these pages). Latin read from the Google djvu OCR and checked against the page image (PDF page) by eye; OCR may still err in individual letters.
english: "The rule of truth which we hold, is, that there is one God Almighty, who made all things by His Word, ... For God needs none of all these things, but is He who, by His Word and Spirit, makes, and disposes, and governs all things, ... He is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, as we shall prove."
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, Buffalo 1885; New Advent text revised by Kevin Knight)
what_it_says: The rule of truth: one God Almighty who made all things by his Word, and "by His Word and Spirit" makes, orders and governs all things; the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
limits: The Spirit appears as co-agent with the Word in creation; the passage does not say how the Spirit is distinct from the Father or the Word, and it is a rule-of-faith summary, not a Trinitarian definition. The ellipses omit the list of visible and invisible things.

greek: Christum et Spiritum sanctum, a quibus consummatos esse dicunt Aeonas. Christum enim docuisse eos conjugationis naturam, innati comprehensionem cognoscentes sufficientes, sive idoneos, esse: declarasse quoque in eis Patris agnitionem, quoniam incapabilis est, et incomprehensibilis, et non est neque videre, neque audire eum nisi per solum Monogenem. [Harvey's line begins with a word-fragment "dentiam Patris," which is omitted here.]
greek_edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857, vol. 1 (Latin; archive.org item sanctiirenilibr01irengoog). Latin read from the Google djvu OCR and checked against the page image (PDF page) by eye; OCR may still err in individual letters. Greek of the same clause (Epiphanius) printed above on p. 21.
english: "...they tell us that Monogenes, acting in accordance with the prudent forethought of the Father, gave origin to another conjugal pair, namely Christ and the Holy Spirit (lest any of the Æons should fall into a calamity similar to that of Sophia), for the purpose of fortifying and strengthening the Pleroma..." (ANF 1.2.5).
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, Buffalo 1885; New Advent text revised by Kevin Knight)
what_it_says: In the Valentinian myth, Christ and the Holy Spirit are a later pair of Aeons produced by Monogenes to strengthen the Pleroma; Irenaeus reports this as the opponents' claim.
limits: This is the opponents' fable, reported by Irenaeus; it shows what he rejects (Christ and Spirit as created Aeons), not his own doctrine. Quoted to define the Gnostic target.

ref: 1.8.5 (ANF; the sentence sits in ANF para. 5); Harvey p. 77 (running head "PERPERAM ALLEGATUS")
greek: Bene igitur dixit, In principio erat Verbum; erat enim in Filio: Et Verbum erat apud Deum: etenim principium. Et Deus erat Verbum, consequenter; quod enim ex Deo natum est, Deus est.
greek_edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857, vol. 1 (Latin; archive.org item sanctiirenilibr01irengoog). Latin read from the Google djvu OCR and checked against the page image (PDF page) by eye; OCR may still err in individual letters. Harvey prints the Greek of John 1:1 (Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ Λόγος) on the same page; not transcribed here.
english: "Very properly, then, did he say, In the beginning was the Word, for He was in the Son; and the Word was with God, for He was the beginning; and the Word was God, of course, for that which is begotten of God is God."
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, Buffalo 1885; New Advent text revised by Kevin Knight)
what_it_says: Irenaeus reads John 1:1 as the Gnostics misread it: the Word is "in the Son" and "God" because what is begotten of God is God, i.e. the Word is divine and generated from the Father.
limits: The Latin is Irenaeus quoting the Gnostic gloss and then correcting it; the "generated" wording is his scriptural argument, not Nicene language. "Erat enim in Filio" shows the Son as the principle in which the Word is.

greek: Manifesta igitur expositionis eorum transfictio. Johanne enim unum Deum exponente [l. Omnipotentem], et unum Unigenitum Christum Jesum annunciante, per quem omnia facta esse dicit, hunc Verbum Dei, hunc unigenitum, hunc factorem omnium, hunc lumen verum illuminans omnem hominem, hunc mundi fabricatorem, hunc in sua venisse, hunc eundem carnem factum, et inhabitasse in nobis:
greek_edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857, vol. 1 (Latin; archive.org item sanctiirenilibr01irengoog). Latin read from the Google djvu OCR and checked against the page image (PDF page) by eye; OCR may still err in individual letters. Harvey's Greek for the same passage (Ἕνα Θεὸν παντοκράτορα ... τοῦτον υἱὸν [l. Λόγον] Θεοῦ ...) is printed above it on p. 82.
english: "The fallacy, then, of this exposition is manifest. For when John, proclaiming one God, the Almighty, and one Jesus Christ, the Only-begotten, by whom all things were made, declares that this was the Son of God, this the Only-begotten, this the Former of all things, this the true Light who enlightens every man, this the Creator of the world, this He ..."
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, Buffalo 1885; New Advent text revised by Kevin Knight)
what_it_says: Irenaeus says John proclaims one God and one Christ Jesus the Only-begotten, and identifies this one as the Word of God, the Son, the Maker and the Light who became flesh; the Gnostics split these names into separate Aeons.
limits: This is Irenaeus's own argument against the Gnostic splitting of Logos, Monogenes and Christ; the verb "exponente" is corrected by Harvey to "Omnipotentem". It shows the identity of the Word with Jesus, not a formal homoousios.

ref: 1.30 (Barbeliotae; ANF 1.30.1-3 region, exact paragraph not matched); Harvey p. 225
greek: Deinde ex primo angelo *[qui adstat Monogeni,] emissum dicunt Spiritum sanctum, quem et Sophiam, et Prunicum
greek_edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857, vol. 1 (Latin; archive.org item sanctiirenilibr01irengoog). Latin read from the Google djvu OCR and checked against the page image (PDF page) by eye; OCR may still err in individual letters. The Latin paragraph is numbered "2." in Harvey's Latin layer and does not line up with the ANF paragraph numbering.
english: Nearest ANF sentence (not an exact match for the Latin): "Below these, again, is the Holy Spirit, and under this superior spirit the elements were separated from each other ... calling him the first woman." (ANF 1.30.1); ANF 1.30.3 says the power "they call Sinistra, Prunicus, and Sophia".
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, Buffalo 1885; New Advent text revised by Kevin Knight)
what_it_says: The Barbeliote system: the Holy Spirit is emitted from the first angel (who stands by Monogenes) and is also called Sophia and Prunicus.
limits: Reports an opponent system; the Latin sentence was located in the OCR and not checked on the page image; the English is not a sentence-level match. Wisdom here is a fallen female Aeon, the opposite of Irenaeus's Wisdom-Spirit in 1.22.1 and 2.2.

greek: ... nullius indigens omnium Deus verbo condidit omnia et fecit; neque angelis indigens adjutoribus ad ea, quae fiunt ... sed ipse in semetipso ... fecit quemadmodum voluit; omnibus consonantiam, et ordinem suum, et, initium creationis donans; spiritalibus quidem spiritalem et invisibilem ... omnia autem quae facta sunt, infatigabili Verbo fecit.
greek_edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857, vol. 1 (Latin; archive.org item sanctiirenilibr01irengoog). Latin read from the Google djvu OCR and checked against the page image (PDF page) by eye; OCR may still err in individual letters. Harvey p. 256 prints a margin reference "MASS. II. ii. 3" (Massuet) where ANF has 2.2.4; ANF numbering used here.
english: "...and that He created and made all things by His Word, while He neither required angels to assist Him ... while He formed all things that were made by His Word that never wearies."
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, Buffalo 1885; New Advent text revised by Kevin Knight)
page: Harvey pp. 255-256 (Latin; the PDF page 455 shows p. 256; p. 255 = PDF 454 not visually checked); ANF page unknown
what_it_says: God made all things by his Word alone, not by angels or any intermediate power; the Latin mentions only the Word (Verbum), with no mention of the Spirit.
limits: BRIEF CORRECTION: the brief attributes "by His Word and Spirit" to 2.2.4-5; the Latin here says "Verbo" only. The "Word and Spirit" formula is in 1.22.1 (I1-02). Also the Spirit is not named as creator in 2.2.4.

ref: 2.2.5 (ANF; Latin "5. Quoniam autem hic Deus est Pater ..."); Harvey p. 256 (margin "Eph. iv.", "Joh. i. 3")
greek: Proprium est enim hoc Dei supereminentiae, non indigere aliis organis ad conditionem eorum, quae fiunt: et idoneus [i. e. Λόγος] est et sufficiens ad formationem omnium proprium ejus Verbum, quemadmodum et Johannes Domini discipulus ait de eo; Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil. ... Et hic ergo a Verbo ejus factus est, sicut scriptura Geneseos dicit, omnia quae sunt secundum nos fecisse Deum per Verbum suum. ... 5. Quoniam autem hic Deus est Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi, et de hoc Paulus Apostolus dixit: Unus Deus Pater, [... ex quo omnia].
greek_edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857, vol. 1 (Latin; archive.org item sanctiirenilibr01irengoog). Latin read from the Google djvu OCR and checked against the page image (PDF page) by eye; OCR may still err in individual letters. Harvey's note 4 on p. 256 records that the Greek MSS of Eph. 4:6 read "καὶ πατὴρ πάντων" and that Irenaeus's text lacks "et ... omnium"; Harvey also prints 1 Cor. 8:6 "εἷς Θεὸς ὁ πατὴρ, ἐξ οὗ τὰ πάντα" on p. 257.
english: "For this is a peculiarity of the pre-eminence of God, not to stand in need of other instruments for the creation of those things which are summoned into existence. His own Word is both suitable and sufficient for the formation of all things ... It too, therefore, was made by His Word ..." and "Now, that this God is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, Paul the apostle also has declared, [saying,] There is one God, the Father, who is above all, and through all things, and in us all." (ANF 2.2.5).
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, Buffalo 1885; New Advent text revised by Kevin Knight)
page: Harvey pp. 256-257 (Latin; the "Unus Deus Pater" clause is on p. 257, not visually checked); ANF page unknown
what_it_says: The Word is the sufficient instrument of creation, and the one God is Father, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ; Irenaeus cites Eph. 4:6 in a form that lacks the Greek "and ... of all".
limits: The Word is the God-given instrument of creation, which Irenaeus contrasts with angels; the Latin is an argument from Scripture and does not treat the Spirit. The Eph. 4:6 wording ("one God, the Father, who is above all") is quoted in ANF; Harvey notes a textual variant in the Greek MSS. Not a Nicene definition.

ref: 2.13.3 (ANF); Harvey p. 282 (margin "MASS. II. xiii. 2", Massuet numbering one lower than ANF)
greek: Multum enim distat omnium Pater ab his quae proveniunt hominibus affectionibus et passionibus: et simplex, et non compositus, et similimembrius, et totus ipse sibimetipsi similis, et aequalis est, totus cum sit sensus, et totus spiritus, et totus sensuabilitas, et totus ennoea, et totus ratio, et totus auditus, et totus oculus, et totus lumen, et totus fons omnium bonorum; quemadmodum adest religiosis ac piis dicere de Deo.
greek_edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857, vol. 1 (Latin; archive.org item sanctiirenilibr01irengoog). Latin read from the Google djvu OCR and checked against the page image (PDF page) by eye; OCR may still err in individual letters. Harvey footnote 3 on p. 282: "Sensus, Nous fuit in Greco" (the Latin "sensus" renders Greek νοῦς). Footnote 4 gives a Greek variant for "sensuabilitas".
english: "For the Father of all is at a vast distance from those affections and passions which operate among men. He is a simple, uncompounded Being, without diverse members, and altogether like, and equal to himself, since He is wholly understanding, and wholly spirit, and wholly thought, and wholly intelligence, and wholly reason, and wholly hearing, and wholly seeing, and wholly light, and the whole source of all that is good ..."
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, Buffalo 1885; New Advent text revised by Kevin Knight)
what_it_says: God is simple and uncompounded, not made of parts or passions as humans are; the Father is wholly spirit, mind, reason and light.
limits: "Totus spiritus" and "totus ratio/sensus" describe God in human-analogy terms (Irenaeus says God is above these predicates); the Latin does not say that the Son or Spirit are distinct persons in these lines. Harvey notes Greek "sensus" = νοῦς.

greek: 4. Est autem et super haec, et propter haec inenarrabilis. Sensus enim capax omnium bene et recte dicetur, sed non similis hominum sensui: et lumen rectissime dicetur, sed nihil simile ei,
greek_edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857, vol. 1 (Latin; archive.org item sanctiirenilibr01irengoog). Latin read from the Google djvu OCR and checked against the page image (PDF page) by eye; OCR may still err in individual letters.
english: "He is, however, above [all] these properties, and therefore indescribable. For He may well and properly be called an Understanding which comprehends all things, but He is not [on that account] like the understanding of men; and He may most properly be termed Light, but He is nothing like that light with which we are acquainted."
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, Buffalo 1885; New Advent text revised by Kevin Knight)
what_it_says: The predicates "understanding" and "light" are applied to God, but God is indescribable and not like human understanding or light.
limits: Apophatic qualification: the names are used "according to the love we bear Him" and are not literal, so the passage does not make the predicates univocal. It does not address the Son or Spirit directly.

greek: Ab hoc enim Logon et Zoen fabricatores hujus Pleromatis dicunt emissos, et Logi, id est Verbi, quidem emissionem ab hominum affectione accipientes, et addivinantes adversus Deum, ... quoniam in hominibus quidem consequenter dicatur; in eo autem qui sit super omnes Deus, totus Nus et totus Logos cum sit, quemadmodum praedixi-mus, et nec aliud antiquius, nec posterius, aut aliud alterius habente in se, sed toto aequali et simili et uno perseverante, jam non talis hujus ordinationis sequetur emissio.
greek_edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857, vol. 1 (Latin; archive.org item sanctiirenilibr01irengoog). Latin read from the Google djvu OCR and checked against the page image (PDF page) by eye; OCR may still err in individual letters. Harvey p. 285 "a Nu" = Greek νοῦς; the text is the same as the printed Latin, hyphen as printed.
english: "...in Him who is God over all, since He is all Nous, and all Logos, as I have said before, and has in Himself nothing more ancient or late than another, and nothing at variance with another, but continues altogether equal, and similar, and homogeneous, there is no longer ground for conceiving of such production in the order which has been mentioned."
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, Buffalo 1885; New Advent text revised by Kevin Knight)
what_it_says: Irenaeus argues that the Gnostic idea of Word emitted from Nous cannot apply to God, who is wholly Nous and wholly Logos, so there is no successive order of emission in him.
limits: The argument is directed against Gnostic emission of the Logos from Nous; it does not formulate a Nicene distinction of persons, and it does not explain how the Logos is distinct from God. Harvey's Latin "a Nu" stands for Greek νοῦς. Not checked against the rest of Book 2.

ref: 2.19.9 (ANF); Harvey p. 321 (running head "VALENTINI IMPIETAS"; margin "MASS. II. xix. 8" as read on the scan)
greek: Quis enim sensum habens, et veritatis vel modicum attingens, sustinebit dicentes, super Demiurgum Deum esse alterum Patrem: et alterum quidem esse Monogenem, alterum autem Verbum Dei, quem et in deminoratione emissum dicunt: alterum autem Christum, quem et posteriorem reliquis Aeonibus cum Spiritu sancto factum esse dicunt: et alterum Salvatorem, ...
greek_edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857, vol. 1 (Latin; archive.org item sanctiirenilibr01irengoog). Latin read from the Google djvu OCR and checked against the page image (PDF page) by eye; OCR may still err in individual letters. Harvey's Latin numbering for this paragraph is "4."; the ANF paragraph is 2.19.9. The margin on the scan reads "MASS. II. xix. 8".
english: "For who that has any intelligence, and possesses only a small proportion of truth, can tolerate them, when they affirm that there is another god above the Creator; and that there is another Monogenes as well as another Word of God, ... and another Christ, whom they assert to have been formed, along with the Holy Spirit, later than the rest of the Æons; and another Saviour ..." (ANF 2.19.9)
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, Buffalo 1885; New Advent text revised by Kevin Knight)
what_it_says: Irenaeus lists the Gnostic multiplication of Father, Monogenes, Word, Christ, Spirit and Saviour as separate beings, and rejects "another god above the Creator".
limits: This is the opponents' multiplication of divine beings, which Irenaeus rejects; it shows which Gnostic claims he refutes and does not itself define the divinity of the Son or the Spirit.

ref: 2.25.4 (ANF); Harvey p. 344 (Latin chapter heading "CAP. XXXVIII": "Ostensio quoniam Demiurgus non sit supergressibilis mente, neque super eum alterum divinitatem esse")
greek: ORDINEM ergo serva tuae scientiae, et ne ut bonorum ignarus super transcendas ipsum Deum, non enim transibilis est: neque super Demiurgum requiras quid sit, non enim invenies. Indeterminabilis enim artifex tuus ... super ipsum alium excogites patrem. Non enim excogitabis, sed contra naturam sentiens, eris insipiens: et si in hoc perseveraveris, incides in insaniam ...
greek_edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857, vol. 1 (Latin; archive.org item sanctiirenilibr01irengoog). Latin read from the Google djvu OCR and checked against the page image (PDF page) by eye; OCR may still err in individual letters. The paragraph before (Latin para. 3) is on the same page; ANF 2.25.3-4 numbering used.
english: "Preserve therefore the proper order of your knowledge, and do not, as being ignorant of things really good, seek to rise above God Himself, for He cannot be surpassed; nor do you seek after any one above the Creator, for you will not discover such." (ANF 2.25.4)
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, Buffalo 1885; New Advent text revised by Kevin Knight)
what_it_says: Do not search beyond the Creator or imagine another Father above the Demiurge; the Creator is not surpassable and God cannot be exceeded.
limits: Directed at Gnostic speculation about a higher Father; it is a warning against speculation and says nothing directly about the Son or Spirit.

ref: 2.26.1 (ANF); Harvey p. 345 (running head "CARITAS AEDIFICAT"; Greek chapter 39 heading)
greek: Melius est ergo et utilius, idiotas et parum scientes existere, et per caritatem proximum fieri Deo, quam putare multum scire, et multa expertos in suum Deum [l. Dominum] blasphemos inveniri, alterum Deum Patrem fabricantes: et ideo Paulus clamavit: Scientia inflat, caritas autem aedificat: Non quia veram scientiam de Deo culparet, alioquin seipsum primum accusaret; ...
greek_edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857, vol. 1 (Latin; archive.org item sanctiirenilibr01irengoog). Latin read from the Google djvu OCR and checked against the page image (PDF page) by eye; OCR may still err in individual letters. The Greek heading and the Greek of the first clause are printed on p. 345 (OCR: "ἀμείνων καὶ συμφορώτερον ... βλασφήμους εἰς τὸν ἑαυτῶν εὑρίσκεσθαι δεσπότην").
english: "It is therefore better and more profitable to belong to the simple and unlettered class, and by means of love to attain to nearness to God, than, by imagining ourselves learned and skilful, to be found [among those who are] blasphemous against their own God, inasmuch as they conjure up another God as the Father. ... Knowledge puffs up, but love edifies." (ANF 2.26.1)
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, Buffalo 1885; New Advent text revised by Kevin Knight)
what_it_says: Knowledge that leads to imagining another God as Father is blasphemy; love is better than learned speculation; the Paul text (1 Cor. 8:1) is read against the knowledge of the Gnostics.
limits: Pastoral and anti-Gnostic, not a Trinitarian argument. It does not explain the Son-Spirit relation. The Latin "alterum Deum Patrem fabricantes" names the Gnostic error.
